where: Section 2, first line (and Section 1 last line)
problem: Section 1 defines outside-in as sensors sitting in the room and looking at the headset. Section 2 then calls Lighthouse "outside-in optical timing", but in Lighthouse the base stations only emit beams and the photodiodes are on the headset, so by the chapter's own definition it is not outside-in. A student cannot tell which definition to use, and this contradicts how the rest of the paragraph describes the hardware.
fix: Say: "Lighthouse puts the emitters in the room and the sensors on the headset. The base stations are fixed and known, but the light is received on the headset, so the sensing itself is inside-out; it is often loosely called outside-in because the reference points are in the room." Or drop the outside-in/inside-out label from Lighthouse and only describe the emitter/receiver split.

problem: "Angles from both stations plus known station geometry fix the 6-DOF pose" and "angles from two stations give 6-DOF pose" are wrong. Each station's X and Y sweeps give two angles from one photodiode, which is a direction, so two stations intersect two rays and fix one point in 3-D. A single photodiode therefore gives position only; orientation needs several photodiodes at known offsets on the headset.
fix: Write: "X and Y angles from one station give the direction of that photodiode from the station. Two stations give two directions, whose intersection fixes that photodiode's position, 3 numbers. Several photodiodes at known offsets on the headset are needed to also get orientation, giving the full 6-DOF pose."

problem: Positive yaw left and positive pitch up match a right-handed set with x right, y up, z pointing back. In that same set positive roll about the front-to-back axis tilts the top of the head to the left, not to the right, so the stated roll sign is inconsistent with the two signs next to it.
fix: Either write "positive roll tilts the head to the left" to keep one right-handed convention, or keep "tilts right" and state clearly that roll is measured with the opposite sign.
